plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 10: Fixed-Axis Rotation
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram of the torque produced by a force acting at a point away from the origin. Thin black axes labeled x toward the lower left, y to the right, and z upward meet at a point marked O. A heavy blue arrow labeled r, with an overhead vector arrow, runs from O down and to the right to a black dot labeled P. At P a red arrow labeled F points to the right and slightly upward, and a dashed line extends the line of r past P; the angle between that dashed extension and F is marked theta, with the same angle theta repeated on the far side of F where the dashed line of action continues to the lower right. A thin segment from near the origin meets that dashed line at a small right-angle square and is labeled r_perp. An orange arrow labeled tau rises straight up from P, standing perpendicular to the plane that holds r and F. Below and to the left, a drawn open right hand repeats the same blue r and red F arrows with curved black arrows wrapping around them to indicate the sense in which the fingers curl. Showing the geometric construction and the hand together supplies both the magnitude of the cross product, fixed by r, F, and theta, and its direction, which here lies along the positive z-axis.

elements: three thin black coordinate axes meeting at origin O: x toward lower-left, y to the right, z straight up, each with arrowhead and label
origin marker labeled O
heavy blue position vector r (with overhead arrow label) from O to point P, lying in the horizontal x-y plane
black dot at P labeled P
red force vector F (with overhead arrow label) originating at P, lying in the horizontal plane, rotated by theta from the extension of r
grey dashed line extending the direction of r beyond P (line of action reference)
grey dashed line of action of F continuing to the lower-right past P
two theta angle arcs with label θ: one between the r-extension dashed line and F, one on the far side of F along the line of action
thin black perpendicular segment r_perp from O to the line of action of F, with a small right-angle square at the foot and label r⊥
orange torque vector τ (with overhead arrow label) rising straight up (+z) from P, length proportional to |r||F|sin(theta)
right-hand-rule overlay: stylized open right hand (skin tone) with curled-finger arrows wrapping from r toward F and a thumb/arrow indicating +z torque direction, shown only in the hand view

interactions.label: Angle θ (between r and F)
interactions.teaches: Rotating F about P changes sin(theta): r_perp and the orange tau arrow grow to a maximum at 90 degrees and collapse to zero when F aligns with r, making the |tau| = rF sin(theta) dependence visible

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching from the r_perp/angle construction to the hand cue links the sense of curling the fingers from r to F with the thumb pointing along the resulting torque direction (+z)
Rotating the scene reveals that tau is perpendicular to the plane containing r and F, confirming the cross-product direction rather than an in-plane arrow

demo_steps.title: Geometric construction
demo_steps.narration: With theta near 35 degrees, r_perp is the perpendicular lever arm from O to F's line of action and the orange tau arrow has moderate length.

demo_steps.title: Maximum torque at 90 degrees
demo_steps.narration: At theta = 90 degrees, F is perpendicular to r so r_perp equals the full length of r and tau reaches its maximum rF.

demo_steps.title: Vanishing torque near alignment
demo_steps.narration: As theta approaches 0, F points along r, r_perp shrinks to zero and the tau arrow disappears — a force through the axis produces no torque.

demo_steps.title: Right-hand rule
demo_steps.narration: In the hand view, curling the fingers from r toward F makes the thumb point up along +z, matching the orange tau direction.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World frame: O at origin; +x screen-lower-left, +y screen-right, +z up. r lies in the horizontal (z=0) plane: P ≈ (1.0, 2.4, 0) world units so |r| ≈ 2.6; draw r as a thick blue (#16457c) arrow O→P. F is a red (#cc2222) arrow of fixed length ≈ 2.2 starting at P, oriented in the z=0 plane at angle theta measured from the +r extension direction; at theta=90 its direction is the in-plane perpendicular (-2.4,1,0) normalized so that r×F points +z. tau = r×F drawn orange (#e8901a) from P straight up, length = |r||F|sin(theta) (scale ~0.5 world-unit per unit torque so the 90-degree arrow is ~2.9 units tall). r_perp is a thin black segment from O to the foot of the perpendicular on F's line of action, length |r|sin(theta), with a 0.18-unit right-angle square at the foot. Dashed grey lines: r-extension beyond P and F's line of action both ways. theta arcs radius ~0.5 at P. Right-hand overlay (hand view only): a simplified hand mesh/skin-tone (#e8c39a) palm near lower-left with two black curved curl arrows around the r-F plane and a thumb arrow along +z. Colors: axes #222222, labels black, r blue #16457c, F red #cc2222, tau orange #e8901a, dashed #888888.
interactionPlan.notes: Build r and F as arrow helpers (cylinder+cone) in the z=0 plane; recompute F direction, tau vector/length, r_perp foot, dashed line-of-action endpoints, and both theta arcs reactively on every theta slider change. Keep tau strictly along +z by construction (cross product of two in-plane vectors). For the toggle, keep both the geometric annotation group (r_perp, right-angle square, theta arcs, dashed lines) and the hand-overlay group in the scene and show/hide them; the r, F, and tau arrows remain visible in both modes. Use a standard isometric camera pose; orbit enabled for inspecting the out-of-plane tau direction.

The cross product r→×F→ also tells us the sign of the torque. In the figure, the cross product r→×F→ is along the positive z-axis, which by convention is a positive torque. If r→×F→ is along the negative z-axis, this produces a negative torque.

The torque is perpendicular to the plane defined by r→andF→ and its direction is determined by the right-hand rule.
